items.topic: Nuclear power plant operation and thermal efficiency
items.definition: Nuclear plants generate electricity the same way coal plants do — heating water into pressurized steam that spins a turbine — but produce that heat via nuclear fission instead of combustion.
items.core_idea: Because the turbine technology is shared with coal plants, nuclear plants follow the same thermal-efficiency rule: higher operating temperature and continuous (non-cycling) operation yield more electricity per unit of fuel, with efficiency ranging roughly 25% for a low-temperature plant up to 50-60% for a larger, hotter one.
key_points: Steam-turbine technology is identical between nuclear and coal plants.
Higher operating temperature raises the fraction of heat energy converted to electricity.
A low-temperature plant may convert only ~25% of heat to electricity; a larger, hotter plant can reach 50-60%.
Plants are most efficient running full-time without letting the water cool overnight.
The key difference from coal is the heat source: nuclear fission vs. combustion.
relationships: Shares turbine/steam technology with coal-fired generation
Efficiency behavior parallels coal plant economics
trading_implications: Nuclear plants economically favor running as baseload (continuous full-time operation) rather than cycling, which affects their bidding behavior and price responsiveness in power markets.
common_misunderstandings: Nuclear and coal plants are often thought of as fundamentally different generation technologies, but the electricity-generating turbine stage is the same; only the heat source differs.

items.topic: Nuclear power emissions and environmental/economic constraints
items.definition: Nuclear fission is not a combustion process, so nuclear plants produce no CO2, but they generate radioactive waste instead, and face fuel-supply and siting constraints coal plants don't.
items.core_idea: Nuclear power trades one environmental problem (CO2 emissions) for others: radioactive waste, difficulty and toxicity of sourcing concentrated uranium fuel, weapons-proliferation concerns tied to the refining process, and grid strain from being built far from consumers due to public opposition to local siting.
key_points: Nuclear fission breaks protons and neutrons from the fuel's nucleus without combustion, so no CO2 is produced.
Radioactive waste is the alternative pollution type produced.
Concentrated uranium fuel is highly toxic.
Large, economically extractable uranium deposits are limited despite uranium being common in the Earth's crust generally.
The refining process for reactor fuel is often similar to that for nuclear weapons fuel, linking reactor construction to weapons-proliferation fears.
Like coal plants, nuclear plants have economies of scale requiring large size, and public resistance to local siting ('not in my backyard') pushes them far from consumer regions, straining the grid.
Nuclear fuel refining techniques are often kept as government secrets.
relationships: Contrasts with coal plant CO2/particulate emissions
trading_implications: Grid strain from long transmission distances between nuclear plants and demand centers is a structural factor in regional power flow and congestion.
common_misunderstandings: Nuclear power is sometimes framed as pollution-free because it lacks CO2 emissions, but the source is clear it produces a different pollutant (radioactive waste) and carries other environmental/economic costs.

items.definition: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large atomic nucleus (e.g., uranium) into smaller particles, either spontaneously (radioactive decay) or induced by humans to happen rapidly.
items.core_idea: Fission occurs naturally as radioactive decay in unstable elements; when humans accelerate this process it is called induced fission, which is easiest to trigger in already-radioactive elements like uranium and plutonium and releases alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma radiation.
key_points: Spontaneous fission (radioactive decay) occurs naturally when an unstable nucleus splits on its own.
Induced fission is the human-accelerated version of this splitting process.
Induced fission is easiest in elements already undergoing radioactive breakdown, such as uranium and plutonium.
Fission releases an alpha particle (two protons + two neutrons), beta particles (a pair of electrons), and gamma radiation (electromagnetic energy).
Almost any atomic nucleus can be split given enough energy, but some nuclei are far more susceptible and require much less energy — these are the substances capable of sustaining a chain reaction.
A chain reaction occurs when energy released from one fission event is sufficient to split a nearby nucleus; if nearby nuclei are stable, no chain reaction results.

Nuclear radiation, a nuclear reactor, and a nuclear bomb differ only in the speed/rate of the fission chain reaction: radiation is slow with no chain reaction, a reactor is a measured-rate chain reaction, and a bomb is an extremely fast uncontrolled chain reaction of all the fuel.
relationships: Underlies the fuel enrichment process (Uranium-235 vs Uranium-238)
common_misunderstandings: Reactors and bombs are sometimes conflated as the same process; the source clarifies the difference is purely the rate of the chain reaction, not the underlying physics.

items.definition: The nuclear cycle is the sequence of stages nuclear fuel passes through: exploration/mining, milling into yellowcake, conversion to uranium hexafluoride gas, and enrichment.
items.core_idea: Raw uranium ore is mined, ground into a powder called yellowcake, converted into uranium hexafluoride (UF6) gas, and then enriched — typically via centrifuge, which uses the mass difference between U-238 and U-235 to concentrate the fissionable U-235 needed to sustain a reaction.
key_points: Stage 1-2: exploration and mining remove uranium-bearing rock from the ground.
Stage 3: at a processing plant, uranium is separated from other rock and milled into a powder called yellowcake.
Stage 4: yellowcake is converted into a gas by combining uranium with fluoride to form uranium hexafluoride (UF6).
Stage 5: enrichment brings the fuel to a desired ratio of fissionable Uranium-235 to nonfissionable Uranium-238.
The most common enrichment method spins UF6 gas in a centrifuge; heavier U-238 moves outward while lighter, fissionable U-235 is collected from the inside.
Most naturally occurring uranium is not enriched enough to sustain a nuclear reaction on its own — enrichment is required to reach a sufficient concentration of U-235.
U-235 is favorable because it fissions easily, releasing more energy than is required to split its nucleus.
relationships: Enrichment ratio determines whether a chain reaction can be sustained
trading_implications: The enrichment/mining supply chain (limited economically extractable deposits, mining, milling, conversion, centrifuge enrichment) is a multi-stage cost and supply-security factor in uranium fuel markets.
common_misunderstandings: Mined uranium is not directly usable as reactor fuel; it must go through milling, conversion, and enrichment before it can sustain fission.

items.definition: Isotopes are variants of an element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons; the atomic mass number is protons plus neutrons, while the atomic number is protons alone.
items.core_idea: Isotopes of an element behave identically chemically but differ in nuclear stability due to differing atomic weight; the number after an element's chemical symbol (e.g., U-235, U-238) denotes the atomic mass number (protons + neutrons), distinct from the atomic number (protons only), which is not shown in a chemical formula.
key_points: Isotopes share the same proton count but differ in neutron count.
Chemically, isotopes of the same element behave identically.
Nuclear stability differs between isotopes because of differing atomic weight.
The number appended to a chemical symbol (e.g., U-238, U-235) is the atomic mass number: protons + neutrons combined.
Protons and neutrons weigh about the same, but only protons carry electrical charge.
The atomic number is the count of protons in the nucleus and is never explicitly shown in a chemical formula.
relationships: Distinguishes U-235 from U-238 in the enrichment process
common_misunderstandings: The number after an element's symbol (mass number) is sometimes mistaken for the atomic number; the source explicitly distinguishes the two.
